item.content: {"url": "https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=computational+methods+for+autonomous+research+question+generation+and+prioritization&format=json&resultType=core&pageSize=4", "scope": "Europe PMC search metadata, abstracts and full-text links; discovery only", "excerpt": "[{\"title\": \"Autonomous AI research agents in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma immunology: from multimodal evidence to experimental validation.\", \"abstract\": \"Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains one of the most challenging malignancies due to profound biological heterogeneity, complex stromal organization, and limited responsiveness to current immunotherapies. Recent advances in single-cell sequencing, spatial omics, digital pathology, and multimodal profiling have revealed that PDAC immune states are shaped not only by cellular composition but also by spatial organization, treatment context, and patient-specific evolutionary trajectories. However, the increasing complexity and fragmentation of biomedical evidence create substantial challenges for conventional artificial intelligence (AI) approaches that are typically optimized for predefined analytical tasks. Autonomous AI research agents represent an emerging paradigm that extends beyond predictive modeling by integrating scientific reasoning, retrieval of heterogeneous biomedical knowledge, computational tool orchestration, workflow adaptation, and evidence traceability. In this Review, we examine how agentic AI systems may contribute to PDAC immunology research, from characterization of immune ecosystems and spatial cellular interactions to biomarker discovery, neoantigen prioritization, and experimental protocol design. We distinguish AI agents from conventional task-specific models and discuss essential capabilities required for reliable biomedical research, including planning, tool use, verification, memory, provenance tracking, and human oversight. Despite promising technical demonstrations in biomedical domains, direct evidence supporting fully autonomous AI-driven discovery and validation in PDAC remains limited. Therefore, we propose a disease-oriented evaluation framework emphasizing benchmark task design, appropriate human and computational comparators, reproducibility assessment, and experimental validation. To evaluate system maturity, we introduce a 6-level \\\"Spectrum of Agentic Autonomy.\\\" We advocate for novel evaluation paradigms centered on full-chain traceability and outline adoption barriers, positioning AI agents as pragmatic scientist-in-the-loop co-pilots.\", \"doi\": \"10.1038/s44386-026-00075-0\", \"pmid\": \"42864384\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13658227\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.1038/s44386-026-00075-0\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13658227\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13658227?pdf=render\"}]}}, {\"title\": \"Artificial intelligence and anti-cancer drugs: advancing discovery, personalization, and precision oncology.\", \"abstract\": \"Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing the way we discover anticancer drugs. It tackles the problems of traditional methods, such as prolonged timelines for drug development, higher costs, and substantial inter-patient heterogeneity. This review explains how AI is applied throughout the cancer drug pipeline. This includes target identification, virtual screening of compounds, molecular docking, and predicting pharmacokinetics. We explore how machine learning models speed up hit-to-lead optimization, improve clinical trial design by stratifying patients, and allow for real-time toxicity monitoring. A key focus is on integrating AI with multi-omics data, including proteomics, genomics, transcriptomics, and metabolomics, to support precision oncology and personalized treatments. We address important validation challenges, like model interpretability, data quality, and regulatory issues that must be solved before AI can be widely used in clinics.
